name: Mysterious Name

human.symptom: Identifiers that don't reveal intent — names like aFunc(), x, theData, temp, or one-letter loop variables that force every reader to reverse-engineer the code's purpose.
human.goal: Names read as the domain — a function's purpose, a variable's role, a class's responsibility — visible in one glance.
human.pressure: Every reading is a re-comprehension cost; bugs sneak in because what code does diverges from what its name suggests. Compounds in proportion to how many readers (humans + LLMs) touch the file.
human.tradeoff: Cross-repo greps, commit history, code comments, and string-literal references to the old name silently drift stale — the team absorbs the rename in PRs they weren't planning to read.
human.relief: Reduces onboarding time, accelerates code review, and lets future-you skim instead of decode.
human.trap: Naming bikeshedding — endless rename churn for marginal clarity gains while the actual code structure stays unimproved.

agent.symptom: Token-level identifiers don't disambiguate scope or domain — the agent must load surrounding context to answer 'what does this variable hold?' before any reasoning step succeeds.
agent.goal: Identifiers carry enough disambiguating information that the agent can reason about each symbol without a lookup hop.
agent.pressure: Every reasoning pass re-derives meaning from surrounding context; chained edits compound the cost and increase the chance of hallucinating a misread.
agent.tradeoff: Renames invalidate cached associations — commit history, RAG snippets, embedding indexes, and prior conversation context all carry the old name until they refresh.
agent.relief: Fewer context-lookup hops per reasoning step; planning loops run cheaper and resist drift.
agent.trap: Compulsive renaming generates spurious diffs that crowd the review surface and burn context the human reviewer has to skim past.

name: Duplicated Code

human.symptom: The same code structure appears in two or more places — same shape with cosmetic variations, or copy-paste-modify patterns that drift over time.
human.goal: One canonical home per behavior, with parameters for the variations.
human.pressure: Bugs need to be fixed in every copy; behavior diverges as copies age, multiplying maintenance cost.
human.relief: A bug fix or enhancement lands once, not in every clone — and the unifying name reveals shared intent.

name: Long Function

human.symptom: Functions whose body has dozens of lines and a mix of concerns — fetching, calculating, formatting, and logging all interwoven.
human.goal: Each function reads as a sequence of named single-responsibility steps; nothing does more than its name advertises.
human.pressure: Each line is an opportunity for the reader to lose context; understanding requires holding the whole function in working memory.
human.tradeoff: Splitting introduces a navigation cost — readers gain named outlines but pay function-jump hops to follow the implementation. The wrong granularity buys clutter without comprehension.
human.relief: Faster to read, easier to test, simpler to change one step without touching the others.
human.trap: A maze of one-line helpers where the workflow can no longer be read linearly — extraction without earning a name fragments the procedure into pieces too small to mean anything.

agent.symptom: A function whose token count exceeds the agent's reliable chunk-reasoning budget; verifying behavior preservation requires re-reading the entire span on every edit.
agent.goal: Each function is a verifiable unit small enough that the agent can reason about its full behavior in a single reasoning step.
agent.pressure: Every edit pays full re-read cost; chained changes compound context usage and increase the chance of missing a cross-statement invariant.
agent.tradeoff: Splitting inflates context-window usage at orchestration time — the agent now loads N function definitions to follow what was once one body. Worth it when the orchestration outline is clearer than the linear body.
agent.relief: Smaller diff surface per commit; behavior preservation verifiable per refactoring step; chained orchestrations work from named subroutines instead of re-derived semantics.
agent.trap: Forces the agent to chase a dozen function definitions for what was once a 20-line procedure — context cost inflates and cross-function invariants disappear.

name: Long Parameter List

human.symptom: Functions taking five, six, or more parameters — especially when several travel together as a logical group.
human.goal: Related parameters travel together as one well-named value object that the function (and its callers) refer to by domain meaning.
human.pressure: Callers must remember argument order and meaning; refactoring becomes a coordination exercise across every call site.
human.relief: Adding a related field is one type change instead of touching every signature; intent is named at the call site.

name: Global Data

human.symptom: Module-level variables, singletons, or shared mutable state that any code can read or mutate from anywhere.
human.goal: Access goes through a small named function that owns the read/write contract — and ideally narrows it (read-only, validated).
human.pressure: The blast radius of any change is the whole codebase; behavior depends on hidden write order between unrelated callers.
human.relief: All access sites become trivially findable; you can add logging, validation, or a cache without touching consumers.

name: Mutable Data
after:
const order = { total: 100 };
const final = addTax(applyDiscount(order));

human.symptom: Data structures whose fields are reassigned across the codebase, with no clear owner of the mutation.
human.goal: Mutation happens in one place behind a named function (or returns a new value), so the moment of change is clear.
human.pressure: Reasoning about state at any moment requires tracing every writer; concurrent code becomes a hazard area.
human.relief: Bugs stop being 'who set this field?' and become local to the encapsulating method.

name: Divergent Change

human.symptom: One module changes for many unrelated reasons — one part for tax law updates, another for UI changes, another for API shape drift.
human.goal: Each module changes for one reason — the kinds of changes that touch it cluster around a single axis of variation.
human.pressure: Every team's churn lands in the same file; merges become contentious; testing one concern requires understanding all of them.
human.relief: Owners and reviewers are obvious; tests are focused; teams can move in parallel without colliding.

name: Shotgun Surgery
before:
// Five files each have:
log(`event=${event}, user=${user}`);

human.symptom: A single conceptual change forces edits in many small places — adding a logging field means touching 17 files.
human.goal: All code that varies together lives together. Adding a new field is one change in one module.
human.pressure: Easy to miss a site; reviewers can't easily verify completeness; small changes feel disproportionately risky.
human.relief: Change cost becomes proportional to the conceptual change, not to how widely the concept was scattered.

name: Feature Envy
after:
class Item  { weight()      { return this.unitWeight * this.qty; } }
class Order { totalWeight() { return this.items.reduce((s, i) => s + i.weight(), 0); } }

human.symptom: A method on class A reaches deeply into class B's data via getters, then computes something B should compute.
human.goal: Methods live with the data they care about — B owns the logic over B's fields.
human.pressure: Domain logic lives where it's least expected; B's internals leak through public surfaces just to support A's method.
human.tradeoff: Moving the method may pull collaborators with it — A's other internals that the moved method referenced now need to travel too, or get passed in as parameters. Sometimes the move uncovers a missing third class.
human.relief: Encapsulation tightens, getters can shrink or disappear, and the method's name clarifies once it's on the right class.
human.trap: Moving every method that reads another class's data — even legitimate cross-class queries — over-tightens encapsulation and forces a fan-out of moves that breaks the original design's intent.

agent.symptom: A method's body references foreign-class data more than its own; the agent loading this method must also load the foreign class to verify any change.
agent.goal: Method bodies stay close to the data they read — the agent loads one class to reason about one behavior.
agent.pressure: Each call to the envious method pulls a second class into the agent's working context; chained reasoning across the boundary compounds the load.
agent.tradeoff: Moving the method may force additional cross-class dependencies the original boundary hid; the agent verifying the move must trace the new coupling at the destination class.
agent.relief: The method's data sits inside the agent's current reasoning context; verifying behavior touches one class instead of two.
agent.trap: Mechanical move-the-method-to-the-data on every cross-class read creates a fan-out the agent must follow at every call site — the cure becomes a worse smell than the original.

name: Data Clumps

human.symptom: The same group of fields travels together everywhere — (street, city, zip), (start, end), (firstName, lastName) — appearing as parameters, fields, or method args.
human.goal: The clump becomes a value object with its own name and its own behavior.
human.pressure: Adding or removing a field of the clump means touching every site; the clump's identity is invisible.
human.relief: Operations on the clump (formatting, validation, equality) live with it; method signatures shrink.

name: Primitive Obsession

human.symptom: Domain concepts represented as raw strings, numbers, or booleans — phone number is a string, money is a number, status is a code.
human.goal: Each domain concept has a small typed home — Money, PhoneNumber, OrderId, Status — that knows its rules.
human.pressure: Validation and formatting scatter across every consumer; the type system can't catch wrong primitives in the wrong slot.
human.relief: Misuse becomes a type error; behavior accretes around the concept; refactoring is local to the wrapper.

name: Repeated Switches
after: event.handle(); // ClickEvent, KeyEvent, DragEvent each implement handle()

human.symptom: The same switch (or if/else chain) over a type code appears in multiple places — adding a new case means hunting them all down.
human.goal: Each case is a class implementing a shared interface; dispatch happens once via a virtual call.
human.pressure: Dispatch logic is duplicated across the codebase; new cases are easy to miss; the type-code couple amplifies.
human.relief: Adding a new case is one new class; the compiler and tests tell you what's missing.

name: Loops

human.symptom: Imperative for/while loops obscuring what the loop is producing — filter, map, reduce mixed together by hand.
human.goal: The transformation reads as a sequence of named operations: filter, map, reduce.
human.pressure: Reader must mentally execute the loop to learn the result; off-by-one errors and accumulator bugs hide in the body.
human.relief: Intent jumps off the page; bugs concentrate on individual steps that are independently testable.

name: Lazy Element
after: const n = user.name;

human.symptom: A class, function, or namespace that exists but does nothing meaningful — a one-line wrapper, an empty subclass, a passthrough method.
human.goal: Trivial wrappers disappear; the call site says exactly what's happening.
human.pressure: Reader pays a navigation cost to discover the wrapper adds nothing; future changes are tempted to add real work to it.
human.relief: Shorter call chains, less indirection to unwrap when reading; one fewer file to maintain.

name: Speculative Generality

human.symptom: Hooks, abstract base classes, configuration knobs, and parameters added 'in case we need them' — but no real call site uses them.
human.goal: The code expresses exactly what it does today — abstraction earns its keep when a real second user shows up.
human.pressure: Tests are forced to cover branches no one exercises; readers learn a vocabulary they don't need; YAGNI debt compounds.
human.relief: Smaller surface, fewer concepts, fewer test branches.

name: Temporary Field
after:
class Order    { ship() { return new Shipment(this); } }
class Shipment { /* owns the track */ }

human.symptom: A class field used by only one method, set to null or default the rest of the time.
human.goal: The temporary state moves to a dedicated class that exists only when it's relevant.
human.pressure: Reader must trace the conditions under which the field is meaningful; null-checks scatter; the field's role is unclear.
human.relief: Null-checks vanish; class invariants tighten; the new class has a clear purpose.

name: Message Chains
before: const street = order.customer.address.street;
after: const street = order.customerStreet();

human.symptom: Long dotted access paths: a.b.c.d.e — every callsite walks the entire object graph.
human.goal: Callers ask the closest object for what they want; the object delegates internally.
human.pressure: Every link in the chain is a coupling point; renaming any intermediate field breaks every consumer.
human.relief: Encapsulation tightens; intermediate objects can change shape without breaking callers.

name: Middle Man
after:
// Expose team directly when the wrapper adds nothing.
manager.team.members();

human.symptom: A class whose methods all delegate straight through to another object — no decisions, no transformations.
human.goal: Callers talk directly to the real object; trivial passthroughs are deleted.
human.pressure: An entire layer of indirection that adds no value; readers must follow every call to the real implementation.
human.relief: Fewer files, shorter call stacks, the implementation's location is obvious.

name: Insider Trading
after:
class A { value() { return this._data.value; } }
class B { read(a) { return a.value(); } }

human.symptom: Modules reach into each other's internals to coordinate behavior, bypassing public interfaces.
human.goal: Cooperation happens through narrow, explicit interfaces; secrets stay secret.
human.pressure: Coupling at the implementation level — refactoring one breaks the other in non-obvious ways.
human.relief: Module boundaries become real; tests exercise the public surface; refactoring is local.

name: Large Class

human.symptom: A class with too many fields and methods — multiple unrelated responsibilities under one type.
human.goal: Each class has one cohesive purpose; methods cluster around fields they actually use.
human.pressure: Cognitive load: every reader pays for fields they don't care about; merge conflicts spike; testing is unfocused.
human.relief: Smaller, more testable units; clearer ownership; faster reading.

name: Alternative Classes with Different Interfaces
before:
class CSVExporter  { writeAll(rows) {} }
class JSONExporter { dump(data)     {} }
after:
class CSVExporter  implements Exporter { write(rows) {} }
class JSONExporter implements Exporter { write(rows) {} }

human.symptom: Two classes do similar things but with mismatched method names and signatures — sortBy() vs orderUsing(), valueOf() vs evaluate().
human.goal: Equivalent operations have equivalent signatures; a shared superclass or interface emerges naturally.
human.pressure: Substitution becomes copy-paste; consumers can't treat the two interchangeably; abstraction over them is impossible.
human.relief: Polymorphic use becomes possible; new alternatives plug in without bespoke adapters.

name: Data Class

human.symptom: A class that holds fields with getters and setters but no behavior — and consumers do all the operations on it externally.
human.goal: Behavior that belongs with the data lives on the class; the class becomes a real domain object.
human.pressure: Domain logic gets scattered to consumers; the class's data invariants aren't enforced; encapsulation is theater.
human.relief: Invariants are enforceable; consumers write less domain plumbing; tests target the class itself.

name: Refused Bequest

human.symptom: A subclass inherits methods or fields it doesn't actually use — overriding to no-ops, throwing 'unsupported', or just ignoring the inheritance.
human.goal: Sharing happens through composition (a delegate object) rather than forced inheritance.
human.pressure: Liskov violations: callers can't trust subclass instances to honor the parent contract; polymorphism becomes a trap.
human.relief: Each class has only what it needs; surprises in polymorphic use disappear.

name: Comments
before:
// charge the customer's stored payment method, including tax
charge(c, t * 1.1);
after: chargeWithTax(customer, total);

human.symptom: Comments explaining what the next block of code does, what a function returns, or how a parameter is meant to be used.
human.goal: Names of functions, variables, and types tell the reader what the comment was trying to say. Comments survive only when WHY is non-obvious.
human.pressure: The code didn't reveal its intent — the comment is patching an unnamed function or unclear variable; comment and code drift over time.
human.relief: No more stale comments; readers trust names; the code is the documentation.
